query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys, the dynamic response (i.e., the balance between strength and ductility) is governed by a strain‐rate and temperature–dependent transition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning. At lower temperatures and higher strain rates, enhanced twin formation contributes to additional strain hardening and increased yield strength, whereas at higher temperatures and lower strain rates, the deformation is dominated by dislocation slip which favors ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast and homogenized Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with minimized casting defects, exhibiting a predominantly single-phase microstructure similar to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
generation.intervention: Prepare specimens via controlled casting and homogenization, then subject them to uniaxial compression or tension tests over a controlled matrix of temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 600 K) and strain rates (from quasi‐static ~10^–3 s^–1 up to dynamic ~10^3 s^–1 using a split‐Hopkinson pressure bar). Complement the mechanical tests with in‐situ high-speed imaging (or digital image correlation) and post-mortem microstructural characterization (TEM and EBSD) to quantify dislocation density and twin fraction.
generation.conditions: Testing in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; temperature set points at 77 K, 300 K, and 600 K; strain rates spanning from ~10^–3 s^–1 (quasi-static) to ~10^3 s^–1 (dynamic) in uniaxial loading experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of dislocation structures and the formation of deformation twins that mediate work hardening.
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic loading, the competition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning modulates the strain-hardening behavior. At low temperatures and high strain rates, the activation energy for twinning is lower relative to slip, causing enhanced twin formation which boosts strength without severely compromising ductility. At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, dislocation slip becomes dominant, resulting in less twinning and a shift towards higher ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens tested at lower temperatures and higher strain rates will exhibit higher twin densities, elevated dynamic yield strengths, and greater strain-hardening rates compared to those deformed at higher temperatures and lower strain rates, where dislocation slip predominates. This adaptive mechanism is predicted to preserve a favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.baseline: The strength–ductility balance observed in equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloys, which, despite complex chemistry, is achieved via a similar interplay of deformation mechanisms.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to as-cast and homogenized FeNiCrMn alloys with low defect populations under testing conditions between 77 K and 600 K and strain rates from ~10^–3 to 10^3 s^–1. Results may differ if the material contains significant microstructural heterogeneities or if testing is conducted outside these temperature and strain-rate limits.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact critical thresholds (in strain rate and temperature) at which the transition from slip-dominated to twinning-dominated deformation occurs, and minor compositional or microstructural variations may shift these thresholds.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of homogenized FeNiCrMn alloy specimens and perform controlled uniaxial compression (or tension) tests across a matrix of temperatures (77 K, 300 K, 600 K) and strain rates (from ~10^–3 to ~10^3 s^–1). Use in-situ high-speed imaging/digital image correlation and conduct post-test TEM/EBSD analysis to quantify dislocation density and twin volume fraction. Compare the mechanical properties (yield strength, strain hardening) with the observed microstructural changes.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to extract dynamic yield strength and work hardening rate.
Quantitative TEM/EBSD assessment of dislocation structures and twin densities.
Mapping strain localization using digital image correlation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under low-temperature and high strain-rate conditions, there is no systematic increase in the volume fraction of twins (relative to high-temperature/low strain-rate conditions) or if the dynamic yield strength and strain hardening do not correlate with the shift from slip- to twinning-dominated mechanisms, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThis paper investigates the effect of strain rate on the mechanical deformation and microstructural development of dual-phase AlCrFe2Ni2 high-entropy alloy during quasi-static and dynamic compression processes. It is revealed that the as-cast AlCrFe2Ni2 alloy is composed of a mixture of FCC, disordered BCC, and ordered B2 crystal structure phases. The alloy shows excellent compressive properties under quasi-static and dynamic deformation. The yield strength exceeds 600 MPa while the compressive strength is more than 3000 MPa at the compression rates of 30% under quasi-static conditions. Under dynamic compression conditions, the ultimate compression stresses are 1522 MPa, 1816 MPa, and 1925 MPa with compression strains about 12.8%, 14.7%, and 18.2% at strain rates of 1300 s−1, 1700 s−1 and 2100 s−1, respectively. The dynamic yield strength is approximately linear with strain rate within the specified range and exhibit great sensitivity. The strong localized deformation regions (i.e., adiabatic shear bands (ASBs)) appear in dynamically deformed samples by dynamic recrystallization due to the conflicting processes of strain rate hardening and heat softening.Keywords: high-entr

Unlike conventional metallic alloys, which are comprised of a base (solvent) and alloying (solute) elements, high entropy alloys (HEAs) are a class of structural alloys first introduced by Cantor et al. and Yeh et al. that consist of multiple principal elements in equiatomic or near equiatomic concentrations. Owing to their multi-principal element compositions, HEAs are characterized by unique combinations of properties, including mechanical strength,,, hardness,, and wear, and corrosion resistance. The use of multiple principal elements in far-from dilute concentrations unlocks infinite possibilities of combinations of properties and functionalities that are not typically found in conventional metallic alloys. Numerous recent studies on 3d transition metal HEAs, such as CoCrFeMnNi,, CoCrFeNi,, CoFeMnNi, CoCrMnNi, and Co0.25Cr0.1Fe2Mn1.35Ni1.3, have explored the impact of temperature,, grain size, alloy composition, strain rate, strain levels, and phase transformations, on the mechanical behavior of these alloys. The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, or so-called Cantor, alloy is a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase alloy that has been regarded as a model system to many single-phase HEAs.
